QUESTION OF THE WEEK - Following the release of better than expected underlying inflation and wages data, economists were asked the probability of a cut in interest rates before the end of November, and beforee the end of the year. Last week, a November cut was seen as just under an even money bet, but the inflation and wages data has seen odds on a November cut firm.

A cut by the end of the year is strongly favoured, even if it is not delivered in November. In fact, many said December was more likely for a cut as at the December board meeting the RBA will be able to consider September quarter capital expenditure and an update on new enterprise bargaining agreements.

CURRENT ACCOUNT DEFICIT - Continuing soft imports data means the September current account deficit should be well received by financial markets, economists said. Despite rising in the last two months, imports remain below their July level and so the trade balance should remain in surplus for the fourth consecutive month. Exports would have to fall by more than 2.6 percent for the trade balance to move back into deficit. While the current account has little impact on monetary policy decisions, a result in line with expectations should reinforce the market's bullish tone on a November interest rate cut.

BUILDING APPROVALS - After the strong growth of the past two months, some pause is expected. Approvals are seen retaining a positive tone in coming months as the effects of two rounds of interest rate cuts are felt. In August, building approvals reached their highest levels in just under a year and are seen as having passed their trough for this cycle.

RETAIL TRADE - After detracting from growth in the June quarter, the strength seen in the first two months of the September quarter means that in the September quarter retail trade is likely to make a fairly large contribution to GDP, economists said. At the same time, the strength seen in the last two months also means that in the month of September, retail trade is likely to register a corrective fall, they said.
